Item / Concern: Shoot-day scheduling methodology: sunlight > equipment > location hierarchy, block-based scheduling, ~12 shots/day
Notes: Salman's framework, endorsed by Nicholas: when scheduling the 30 total shots, prioritize (1) sunlight conditions - the most uncontrollable variable, (2) camera/equipment setup - minimize rig changes between shots, then (3) location - least prioritized. Nicholas recommends block-based scheduling: group shots into blocks sharing the same lighting condition or equipment setup rather than scheduling strictly chronologically or by location; blocks can then be moved between days as needed (outdoor conditions make rigid chronological scheduling impractical). Dream/surreal sequences have more flexibility since they don't need to match continuous lighting. Scene-cohesion rule: film each distinct scene as a cohesive block even if spread across two days, rather than splitting halves across incompatible times. Sam estimates a comfortable pace of ~12 shots/day: proposed 12 Saturday, 12 Sunday, 5-6 Monday pickups (all 30 shots are longer takes). Location count: ~4-5 spots within the same park, furthest ones 8-12 minutes' drive apart (some walkable, though gear may still need driving); Salman/Nicholas recommend naming or numbering each location to simplify scheduling communication.

Item / Concern: On-set take/timing protocol
Notes: ADs will track shot duration on set and report elapsed time and flag significant overruns (e.g. a 40-second target becoming 55+ seconds prompts discussion) but will not call cut or override the directors' judgment on when a take feels right; minor overruns (40s target -> 45s actual) don't trigger an automatic redo. Nicholas's recommendation: start rolling earlier than needed and stop later than needed, since raw metric timing alone can't capture performance/rhythm - timing is a rough flag, not a precision constraint (the real rhythm judgment happens in the edit, cross-ref PW-32/PW-41). Salman's recommendation: directors should watch takes on a monitor rather than in person, to judge the shot close to its final form. "Don't call cut" strategy: Sam should not cut until explicitly told, and directors should wait ~10 seconds after a take feels done before calling cut, to preserve breathing room at the end; "resetting" (stopping/restarting without a hard cut call) is also valid to save battery/storage. Nicholas noted he once called cut 2 seconds too early on his own film and regretted it.
